newsitem.title: RUSSIA: OLYMPICS-RUSSIA STEPS UP ST PETERSBURG OLYMPIC BID.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-RUSSIA STEPS UP ST PETERSBURG OLYMPIC BID.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin called on top government officials on Wednesday to beef up their bid to bring the 2004 Olympics to Russia's second city St Petersburg or face the sack.
"We, the heirs of Peter the Great, must do all we can so that St. Petersburg will be suitably presented," he said, invoking the tsar who founded the city in 1703.
"It's a huge responsibility for the government and the people of Russia," Chernomyrdin told the Russian Olympic organising committee, which includes top government officials.
"If you have people on your staffs who have doubts, they aren't the right people. They should be dismissed," he said.

The canal-lined metropolis of five million is one of 11 cities, including Rome, Cape Town and Stockholm, vying for the 2004 games. The International Olympic Committee will decide on a short list in March, and the winner in September.
Experienced observers of the selection process say St Petersburg is an outsider in the contest.
But Chernomyrdin said the timing was right for St Petersburg, historically Russia's "Window on the West", because it will celebrate its 300th anniversary in 2003.
Russia's new economic reforms will also benefit overall by reopening that window through Olympic sponsorship, he said.

Russia will have to overcome not only staffing problems to win the 2004 bid. The former tsarist capital on the Baltic, home to some of Russia's most impressive architecture and the fabulously rich Hermitage art gallery, has fallen into neglect in recent years and is in need of major restoration.
As part of the campaign for St Petersburg's bid, Russian officials on Wednesday unveiled several new posters, including one offering 15 reasons in support of the city.
"All the major events in recent decades held in Russia, and in St. Petersburg in particular, were perfectly peaceful and environmentally friendly," was one reason.
Moscow held a widely praised Olympics in 1980, although the games were marred by a U.S. boycott in protest at the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

But the organisation of the smaller Goodwill Games, held in St. Petersburg in 1994, was criticised by some competitors. The ice on the skating rink melted and some swimmers refused to take part because the pool was murky.
